title: The Woman, the Child, and the Dragon
summary: A woman clothed with the sun cries out in labor while a great red dragon waits to devour her child. The child, who will rule the nations, is caught up to God, and the woman flees to the wilderness, where God nourishes her. Michael and his angels throw the dragon, the ancient serpent called the devil and Satan, down from heaven; a heavenly voice declares that believers have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb, and the enraged dragon turns to make war on the woman's other children.
story: The seventh trumpet (11:15-19) announced that God's kingdom had come. Chapter 12 now steps back to show the deep story behind everything the churches have suffered. The conflict is older than Rome and larger than any persecution: it runs back to the serpent of Genesis 3 and forward to the end. The chapter tells, in a single picture, the birth, ascension, and victory of the Messiah, the defeat of Satan, and the reason the church still suffers: the dragon has lost, knows his time is short, and is furious. Chapter 13 will show the agents through whom he wages his war, the two beasts.
historical:
Readers in the province of Asia knew stories like this one. Many scholars have noted its resemblance to the Greek myth of Leto, who was pursued while pregnant by the serpent Python and gave birth to the god Apollo, who later killed the serpent; Ephesus claimed that the birth took place in a grove near the city. Egypt told of Isis, pursued by the monster Set while protecting her son Horus. Emperors sometimes associated themselves with Apollo. If John's hearers caught the echo, the point would be pointed: the true child who defeats the dragon is not an emperor but Jesus, and the true dragon stands behind the empire, not against it.

The chapter's images are grounded chiefly in Israel's Scriptures, however, and the historical question it answers is why believers suffer after the Messiah's victory. Jesus was born, died, rose, and ascended in the first third of the first century, yet his people were still being hunted: by local hostility, by Nero's persecution in Rome after AD 64, and by pressures in Asia. The chapter's answer is that the dragon's fury is the rage of a defeated enemy with little time.
cultural:
The woman's crown of sun, moon, and twelve stars recalls Joseph's dream, in which his father, mother, and eleven brothers appear as sun, moon, and stars (Genesis 37:9), so she is linked to Israel and its twelve tribes. The prophets pictured Zion as a woman in labor giving birth to a new people (Isaiah 26:17; 66:7-8; Micah 4:10). The dragon has deep roots. The Old Testament speaks of Leviathan and Rahab, sea monsters that God crushes (Psalm 74:13-14, which mentions Leviathan's heads; Isaiah 27:1; 51:9), and Ezekiel 29:3 calls Pharaoh the great dragon in the midst of his rivers. Texts from ancient Ugarit, a Canaanite city on the Syrian coast, describe a seven-headed sea serpent. The ten horns come from Daniel's fourth beast (Daniel 7:7), and the stars swept down recall Daniel 8:10.

Michael is the angel who stands guard over Israel in Daniel 10:13 and 12:1. Satan is a Hebrew word meaning adversary or accuser, and in Job 1 to 2 and Zechariah 3:1 the satan accuses God's servants before him. The eagle's wings recall God's words at Sinai, that he carried Israel on eagles' wings (Exodus 19:4), and the wilderness, where God fed Israel with manna, becomes the place of the woman's protection. The earth opening its mouth echoes Numbers 16:30-32 and the song of the sea in Exodus 15:12.
literary: Chapter 12 opens a new section of the book (chapters 12 to 14) that many see as its center. It is introduced by a great sign in heaven, the first time Revelation uses that word for a vision. The chapter has three panels. The first (vv. 1-6) is the woman, the dragon, and the child. The second (vv. 7-12) is the war in heaven, interpreted by a hymn. The third (vv. 13-17) returns to the woman on earth. The hymn in the middle is the key: what looks like an angelic battle is explained as the result of the Lamb's blood and the believers' testimony. The story leaps from birth to ascension without narrating the life of Jesus between, compressing the whole gospel into a single verse. The protection of the woman for 1,260 days, or a time, times, and half a time, repeats the period of chapter 11, a limited season of pressure under God's care.

outline.t: The woman, the dragon, and the child caught up to God
War in heaven: the dragon thrown down
The victory hymn: conquered by the blood of the Lamb
The dragon pursues the woman and her children

doctrines.note: The accuser is thrown down, and believers conquer him “by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony.” Christ's death answers every accusation against his people, and Satan's power to condemn them is broken.
The church suffers not because Satan is winning but because he has lost. His fury is intense because he knows his time is short. This does not make suffering easier, but it changes its meaning.

The woman, protected in the wilderness, and her other children who keep God's commandments and hold to the testimony of Jesus, picture God's people as one family across both covenants, pursued yet preserved.

words.note: Drakōn, dragon, a great serpent. In the Greek Old Testament it translates the sea monsters and Leviathan. Revelation identifies it plainly in verse 9 with “that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan”, joining the serpent of Genesis 3 with the chaos monster of Israel's poetry.

Katēgōr, accuser, a legal term for a prosecutor. Its Hebrew counterpart is the satan of Job and Zechariah. The accuser's work was to charge God's people before him day and night. His expulsion means there is no longer any court in which believers can be condemned (compare Romans 8:33-34).

Nikaō, to conquer, overcome, win a victory. Each of the seven churches was promised a reward for the one who conquers (chapters 2 and 3). Here conquering is redefined: the saints conquer by the Lamb's blood and their testimony, and by not loving their lives so much that they shrink from death.

Sēmeion, sign. Revelation uses it for visions that point beyond themselves (here and 15:1) and for the deceptive signs of the beast (13:13-14). The woman and the dragon are signs: symbols to be understood, not literal figures in the sky.

christ: The male child “who will rule all the nations with an iron scepter” is Jesus, in the words of Psalm 2:9, the psalm of the Messiah whom God sets on Zion. The chapter tells his story in a flash: born of Israel, threatened by the dragon (as Herod sought to kill the infant Jesus, Matthew 2:16), caught up to God and his throne in the ascension. It then says what his work achieved: the accuser is thrown down, and salvation, power, and kingdom have come with the authority of God's Christ. Jesus spoke of seeing Satan fall like lightning (Luke 10:18) and said that the ruler of this world would be driven out when he was lifted up on the cross (John 12:31-32). The chapter is also one of the New Testament's fullest echoes of Genesis 3:15, where God promised that the woman's offspring would crush the serpent.

hard.q: Who is the woman, and when was Satan thrown out of heaven?
hard.a:
The woman has been read as Israel, the people from whom the Messiah came (the twelve stars and the labor imagery of Zion point this way); as Mary, the mother of Jesus, a reading developed especially in Catholic and Orthodox tradition; and as the church, who is persecuted after the child ascends and whose children keep the testimony of Jesus. Many interpreters conclude that she is the one people of God, Israel giving birth to the Messiah and continuing as the church, with Mary as the historical mother in whom that people bore its child. The text's symbolism allows these layers, and readers across traditions have held them together.

The timing of Satan's fall is also debated. Some read the war in heaven as a primordial rebellion before creation or before the fall of humanity, drawing on passages like Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28 (which in context speak of the kings of Babylon and Tyre). Futurists often place it in the final period. Many others read it as the heavenly side of the cross, resurrection, and ascension, since the hymn says the saints conquered by the blood of the Lamb and Jesus linked Satan's fall to his own ministry and death (Luke 10:18; John 12:31). These positions are held by faithful readers; the chapter's claim, that the accuser is defeated, stands on each.

questions: The dragon rages because he knows his time is short. How does it change your view of hardship to see it as the fury of a defeated enemy?
The saints conquer by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony. What would conquering look like in your life on those terms?
The accuser charges God's people day and night. What accusations do you still listen to that Christ's death has already answered?
